# AGENT.md: make this person's booking page and its film You are a coding agent working for one person who sells their time: a freelancer, a consultant, a coach, a tutor, a therapist, an adviser. They picked this format: a page whose first screen is **a week of their diary**, set like a good week-to-view, with their name and "I help … with …" in the margin and the ways to work with them under it. That week plays as a short film of a visitor booking: an offer is picked (the times too short for it fade, the ones that fit are inked round), Thursday at ten lights, a slip tucked into the diary is written in (a name, one line about the problem), Confirm, and **the invite card falls into the week** and settles into the slot as an entry. Under the film: the offers drawn as lengths of time, how working together goes, proof slots, a short FAQ, and the **real booking** (their scheduler's embed, both time zones side by side, an email fallback). The same page opened with `?record&ratio=16:9` is the stage they record for X. The page only works if everything on it is **theirs**: their offers at the lengths they sell them, their real hours, their words, their clients' real words. You are gathering what already exists, not writing a persona. Never invent an offer, a rate, a client, a logo, a testimonial, a number or a credential. If something is missing, leave the placeholder and ask. Read `tour/README.md` once for the engine's vocabulary (the parts that matter here: `data-tour-frame`, *A second design size for tall stages*, *A third for squarish stages*, `type` with `rhythm: 'human'`, `stream`, `mark`). Then work through this in order. ## 0. Where things are ``` index.html the page. Its markup is yours to edit: the film (the diary inside the frame, the rail under it), then the offers, how it goes, proof, questions, the booking, the footer kit/ placeholder kit: tokens, .ph frames, buttons, notes (press N to hide notes) office-hours/section.css the stage, the rail, the diary in its three layouts, and the page (.oh-…) office-hours/script.js the film: three chapters, the offer it picks, what the visitor writes office-hours/section.js fills the coming week's dates, plays the film once it's on screen, the booking's logic office-hours/section.html the markup as it came (index.html has a filled-in copy; edit index.html) tour/ the engine (tour.js, tour.css), snapshot.py, README.md; don't edit ``` (In the StyleFeatures repo, `python3 templates/scaffolds/sections/demo/tour/export.py --format office-hours` makes this layout.) Serve the folder with any static server, e.g. `python3 -m http.server 8000`. ## 1. Gather their things (before writing anything) Ask the person for what you can't find, and confirm anything you found before it goes public. Look in this order: - **Their booking link.** Cal.com, SavvyCal, TidyCal, Calendly, Acuity, Google Calendar appointment pages, Zcal, a `book`/`call` page on their site, the link in their email signature. Note **one URL per offer** if their tool has separate event types (`cal.com/name/intro`, `cal.com/name/session`), and whether it can be embedded (most give an inline-embed URL or snippet). That link is the ending of the page; the diary on top is a picture of it. - **Their offers.** The event types in that tool are the honest list: name, length, the description they wrote. Also their site's Services / Work with me / Coaching page, a rate card PDF, a proposal template. Take **two or three**, with the **lengths they really sell** ("20 min", "45 min", "3 h", "a day"). Rates **only if they already publish them**; otherwise the rate line is deleted, never estimated. - **Their hours.** When they actually take calls: which days, which hours, which time zone (an IANA name such as `Europe/Lisbon`, `America/New_York`). Their scheduler's availability settings say this exactly. Ask what they never do ("no calls on Friday afternoons", "mornings are for writing"): that becomes the handwritten note in the diary. - **Who they help, with what.** Their bio on LinkedIn, X, their site's About, their newsletter. You need one sentence in the shape "I help *who* with *what*", in their words, shortened if it must be, never rewritten into marketing. - **How working together goes.** What happens before a call (a questionnaire? nothing?), on it, after it (notes, a plan, a recording, an invoice) and when. Their onboarding email or welcome doc usually has it. - **Proof.** Testimonials they already publish (their site, LinkedIn recommendations, Google reviews, a Senja/Testimonial wall), with the person's name and role. **Only real ones, and only with permission.** Client logos only where the client agreed to be named. If there are none, delete the proof section; don't leave fakes. - **Questions people really ask.** Their FAQ page, or ask them for the three questions they answer most in email. - **Their look.** If they have a site, take its fonts and its one accent colour (CSS variables, a theme file) and set `--oh-ink` (the fountain-pen blue) to it. Otherwise keep the kit's warm paper and the ink. Therapists, coaches and anyone working with private clients: the diary shows **patterns, not people**. Busy time is hatched and never labelled, and nothing on the page hints at who else is in the week. ## 2. Fill the diary (inside the frame) The diary is `.oh-diary` inside `[data-tour-window]` in `index.html`, built in design pixels with three layouts from one set of markup (`office-hours/section.css`): **wide** 1200 × 740 (margin on the left, Monday–Friday), **square** 800 × 700 (`.is-square`: the margin becomes a band over the week; 1:1 recordings) and **tall** 480 × 800 (`.is-tall`: the margin on top, Wednesday–Friday only; phones and 9:16). Check all three after every change. - **The margin** `.oh-margin`: `.oh-name` (their name exactly as they write it), `.oh-help` ("I help … with …"), and the offers `.oh-offer` ×2–3: `data-len` is the length in minutes (it decides which times fade in the film), `data-name` the name, then the name, the length as they say it, and one short line. Keep the `data-tour="offer-…"` hooks. The little month and "Times in …" are filled by `section.js`. - **Time zone.** Put their IANA zone on the root: `
`, and replace every "your city's time" with how they'd say it ("Lisbon time"). With `data-tz` empty the page uses the visitor's own zone. - **The week** `.oh-cols`: one `.oh-col` per day. Each time is a box with `style="--s:10;--m:60"` (start in hours, 13.5 = 13:30; length in minutes) and its label. Open times: `10:001 h`. Busy: ``, no text. Draw **their real pattern** for a typical week, not their actual appointments. The grid runs 9:00–17:00 (`--h0:9;--hours:8` on `.oh-diary`, and the hour labels in `.oh-hours`); change all three together for other hours. - **The booked time** `[data-tour="slot-thu"]` is the one the film books. It holds the lit band, the entry it becomes, the slip, the invite card and the camera's zone. Move the whole element to another day or hour if Thursday at ten isn't a time they'd offer; `section.js` reads its column and label for every date on the slip and the card. - **The handwritten note** `.oh-hand`: one thing they never do, in their words, or delete it. - **The invite card** `.oh-invite`: the offer's name, `{{call_how}}` (how calls happen: "Video call · the link is in the invite", "Phone call · I'll ring you", "At the studio, 12 Example Street" only if they meet in person and say so). - Dates fill in from the coming week. To pin a week (for a recording you'll redo later), set `data-week="2026-11-09"` on the root. **Static HTML/CSS only** inside the frame. The diary is a picture the film moves; the real booking is at the end. ## 3. The script (`office-hours/script.js`) It tells the booking in three chapters (*what you need*, *a time that suits*, *in the diary*), about 33 s. Adjust it to them rather than rewriting it: - `FILM_OFFER` is the offer the visitor picks: their most common one, usually the middle one. - `WHO` and `ABOUT` are what the visitor writes on the slip. Keep `WHO` a plain first name and make `ABOUT` the kind of thing their clients really bring them, in a client's words ("Our launch plan needs a second pair of eyes", "My daughter's maths exam is in May", "We need a pricing model before the board meeting"). Never a real client's name or problem. - Chapter titles (a few words, one ``) and captions (one short sentence per action) in their voice. - Every action visibly changes something; one push-in per chapter, then `unzoom()`. `mark('still')` is the frame reduced motion shows: the week with the entry written in. ## 4. Fill the page under the film - **The rail** under the frame: `.oh-band` (`{{band_title}}`, `{{band_line}}`) and the closing frame `.oh-end` (name, their booking address and email, shown at the end of the recording). - **Offers** `#offers`: each `.oh-off` with `style="--m:45"` (minutes, drawn on a three-hour rule), the length set large, the name, two plain sentences on what happens and what they leave with, who it's for, the rate **only if published**, and "Book this" (`data-offer` = its index, which picks it in the booking). - **How it goes** `#how`: three steps, dated the way they'd say it ("Before", "On the call", "Within two days"). - **Proof** `#proof`: real logos (SVG or a clean PNG on transparent, grey them with `filter: grayscale(1)` if they're loud) and one real quote with name and role, or delete the section. - **Questions** `#faq`: three to five, answered in two sentences each. - **The booking** `#book`: put their scheduler's embed URL on `.oh-embed`: `data-embed="https://cal.com/name"` for one link, or `data-embed-0`, `-1`, `-2` for one per offer (the picker switches between them). `section.js` puts it in an iframe; use the tool's **inline embed** URL (Cal.com: the event URL with `?embed=true` or their embed snippet's link; SavvyCal and TidyCal: the inline embed link). If their tool only offers a script snippet, paste it inside `.oh-embed` in place of the `.ph` and leave `data-embed` empty. If they have no scheduler, delete `.oh-embed`: the email fallback (with the offer and any time picked in the diary) becomes the booking. - Clicking an open time or an offer in the diary (after or during the film) brings the visitor here with it chosen, and the email fallback carries it. Keep the open times honest for that reason. - Delete every ``, set the page `` ("Name: book a call") and the meta description (their "I help … with …" line). ## 5. Check it - `index.html?t=14` freezes any moment. Check the middle of each chapter and just after each action: the cursor sits on what it clicked, the times that fade are the ones too short, the slip is whole inside the frame, the card lands squarely on the time and becomes the entry. - `?record&ratio=16:9&t=…`, `?record&ratio=1:1&t=…`, `?record&ratio=9:16&t=…`, and the page at 1440 × 900 and on a 390-wide phone: no sideways scroll, nothing important cut, the diary legible. - With reduced motion: one calm frame, the week with the entry written in. - Nothing left that is lorem, a placeholder you meant to replace, a rate they don't publish, a testimonial without permission, or a hint of who their other clients are. ## 6. Hand it over: record and post End by giving the person this, with the link filled in: 1. Open **`index.html?record&ratio=16:9`** (served, e.g. `http://localhost:8000/?record&ratio=16:9`) in a browser window large enough for a crisp stage: 1920 × 1080 or larger on a Retina display. 2. Record it with **Monet Shot**: choose the browser window, crop to the stage, park the real pointer off the window (the film draws its own cursor). It holds on the first frame for 1.2 s, plays once and stops on the closing frame. Monet Shot adds no zooms of its own, because the clicks aren't real; if you'd rather place zooms on its timeline, open `?record&ratio=16:9&camera=off` so you don't get both. 3. Export H.264 MP4 and post it to X with one line and the link to the booking. **16:9** reads best on desktop and in quote posts; `ratio=1:1` takes more of the phone feed; `ratio=9:16` is for stories. Record each ratio separately; the diary lays itself out again for each, so never crop one into another. 4. X takes MP4 (H.264, AAC) up to 2 min 20 s and 512 MB. The captions are burned in, because X autoplays muted. ## The painting it sits on Opened on its own, the page sits on *Irises* by Vincent van Gogh (public domain), the way Monet Shot frames a take: the site is a sheet with rounded corners and the painting fills the margin. It lives in `backdrop/` (`painting.webp` and a small `backdrop.js`). It turns itself off with `?record` (Monet Shot adds its own painting), with `?bare`, and inside a frame. Keep it, swap `painting.webp` for another, or delete the `backdrop.js` script line in `index.html` to drop it. ## When it's done: record your launch video with Monet Shot [Monet Shot](https://monetshot.pages.dev/) is a free screen recorder, made for pages like this one: it frames every take on a painting and zooms where things happen. Download it for [Mac](https://github.com/SocialAcolyte/monet-shot/releases/download/v0.1.1/MonetShot-0.1.1.zip), [Windows](https://github.com/SocialAcolyte/monet-shot/releases/download/desktop-v0.1.1/MonetShot-0.1.1-windows-x64-setup.exe) or [Linux](https://github.com/SocialAcolyte/monet-shot/releases/download/desktop-v0.1.1/MonetShot-0.1.1-x86_64.AppImage) (Windows and Linux are test builds; other packages are on the [releases page](https://github.com/SocialAcolyte/monet-shot/releases)). 1. Open the finished site with `index.html?record&ratio=16:9&captions=on` (use `ratio=1:1` or `ratio=9:16` for square and vertical posts). Only the stage shows, it plays once from the start, and captions are on, because X autoplays muted. 2. In Monet Shot, pick the browser window, crop to the stage, and park your real pointer off it (the tour draws its own cursor). Record one play-through. 3. Export, and post it with a link to the site. **For the agent:** when the site is finished, end your last message to the person with this step: the full `index.html?record&ratio=16:9&captions=on` link on their real URL (and the 1:1 and 9:16 versions), and the Monet Shot download link above for their computer.

# tour.js: the demo-film engine One engine for every StyleFeatures demo film. A template supplies a window with a product inside it and a script; the engine plays it with a fake cursor, a camera, chapter cards and captions, and drives it from a scroll, a clock, a screen recorder or a frozen `?t=`. Files: | file | what it is | edit it? | |---|---|---| | `tour.js` | the engine: step builders, `Tour`, `include()` | no, it's shared by every format | | `tour.css` | the engine's look: chromes, cursor, card, caption, keys, controls, record stage | no; restyle through its tokens | | `script.js` | this film's script | yes | | `section.html` / `section.css` | this film's band, closing frame and product | yes | | `snapshot.py` | harvests a live screen into a static fragment | no | | `export.py` | copies the whole format out as a standalone folder | no | | `AGENT.md` | the brief for the coding agent that fills it in | read it | Everything on screen is a pure function of one number, `t`, in seconds. Each frame the engine works out the product's state at `t` (classes, attributes, text, CSS variables, scroll positions), the camera, the cursor and the overlays, then writes only what changed. Nothing depends on what happened in earlier frames, so any moment renders on its own, the same way every time. ## Markup ```html
… your product, built at 1200 × 750 design pixels …
…
…
``` The engine adds the chrome, the cursor, ripples, the chapter card, the caption line, key caps, and the driver's controls. The opening band (`data-tour-band`) slides away in the first `intro` seconds; the closing frame (`data-tour-end`) gets `--in` 0→1 at the end and its own CSS decides what that looks like. The root also carries `--tour-band` (1 → 0 over the intro), `--tour-out` (0 → 1 over the outro) and `--tour-p` (0 → 1 over the whole film) for a format's own CSS. `data-tour-band="css"` stops the engine sliding the band away; the format fades or moves it from `--tour-band` instead. **A frame the format draws: `data-tour-frame`.** Put an element with `data-tour-frame` in the stage and lay it out in CSS (a phone's glass, a mat around a screenshot, a different box per ratio). The engine fits the window to it exactly, clips the camera to it (with its `border-radius`), and every zoom stays inside it: the window always covers the frame, so a push-in never shows what's around it. The outro then leaves the window where it is (use `--tour-out` to do something else). Give the frame the window's aspect ratio. `demo/phone` (the glass, beside the text or under it) and `demo/launch-note` (a mat on the page, a different box per recording ratio) use it. ### Window chromes: `data-chrome` | value | looks like | typical `data-size` | |---|---|---| | `browser` | traffic lights, back/forward, an address pill (`data-url`), share/new icons | `1200x750` | | `app` | a macOS title bar with traffic lights and a centred `data-title` | `1200x760` | | `phone` | a dark bezel, a status bar with the time and a notch | `390x844` | | `none` | just rounded corners | anything | | `terminal` | a warm charcoal window, traffic lights, a centred `data-title`; tokens `--tour-term-bg/-bar/-ink/-dim` | `780x548` | **Windows inside the window.** Any element inside the window with a `data-chrome` gets that chrome too, and a frame (`display:flex`, rounded, clipped). With `data-chrome="none"` on the outer window (made transparent in your CSS) it becomes a desk holding, say, a terminal and a browser; the camera pans between them with `zoom()` (`demo/terminal` does this). **A second design size for tall stages.** `data-size-tall="440x820"` on the window (or `sizeTall: [440, 820]` in the script) is used whenever the stage is taller than wide (W/H < .8: phones, 9:16 recordings). The root gets `.is-tall` before anything is measured, so your CSS can re-lay the product for it (stack two panes, say) and the script's targets follow. `demo/split` stacks its panes this way. **A third for squarish stages.** `data-size-square="760x760"` (or `sizeSquare: [760, 760]`) is used when .8 ≤ W/H < 1.15 (1:1 recordings, square-ish windows), and the root gets `.is-square` the same way. Without it those stages use the wide size, as before. `demo/agentic` has all three: a tiled desk (wide), and one live window beside (square) or above (tall) its run sheet. **A height that follows the frame: `auto`.** `data-size="580xauto"` (or `size: [580, 'auto']`, and the same for `sizeTall`) fixes the window's width and takes its height from the `data-tour-frame` at every layout, so the window always has the frame's shape: a full-height column on a wide page, the whole screen on a phone, any recording ratio. For products that read top to bottom (a chat, a feed, a transcript). `demo/chat` and `demo/mcp` use it. Build the product at the design size in plain CSS pixels. The engine scales the whole window, so text stays real text and stays sharp at any zoom. ### Hooks `'@name'` anywhere in a selector means `[data-tour="name"]`. Put `data-tour="…"` on the things the script points at. Pointer targets also choose the cursor: links, buttons, `role=button|tab|switch` get the hand, inputs and `data-tour-cursor="text"` get the I-beam, the rest the arrow (`data-tour-cursor="arrow|pointer|text"` overrides it). While the cursor rests on a target, that target has `.is-hover`; while it's pressed, `.is-press`. Style both so clicks read. ## The script ```js import { click, type, show, hide, set, tween, zoom, unzoom, chapter, caption, pause } from './tour.js'; export default { size: [1200, 750], // window design size (or data-size on the window) enter: [.84, .97], // where the cursor comes in from, as fractions of the window intro: 1.3, // seconds for the opening band to clear (0: no band) outro: 4.5, // seconds held on the closing frame settle: .6, // pause between the last step and the outro still: 17.4, // the moment reduced motion shows fit: [.92, .88, .5], // optional: see below steps: [ … ], }; ``` `fit: [w, h, y]` is for a stage that holds nothing but the window (a panel beside text, with no card or band over it): the window may take `w` of the stage's width and `h` of its height, centred at `y` (default .5), and push-ins aim at the middle of the frame. Without it the page layout leaves room for the card and band (`[.74, .7, .47]`). It never changes `?record`. `demo/chapters` uses it. Steps run in order on one clock. **Pointer steps** take time and the next step waits for them. **Side steps** start at the current moment and the next step starts with them, so `click('@create'), hide('@modal'), show('@toast')` hides the modal and shows the toast as the click lands. Every step takes: `at: 12.5` pin it to an absolute time · `wait: .4` start this much later · `parallel: true` (pointer steps) don't hold up the next step · `block: true` (side steps) do hold it up. ### Pointer steps | step | what happens | options (defaults) | |---|---|---| | `move(sel)` | glides there on a gentle arc, smootherstep | `dur` .9, `aim` [x, y] fractions of the target, `cursor` | | `click(sel)` | moves, presses (cursor shrinks, target gets `.is-press`), ripple | as `move` | | `dblclick(sel)` | moves, two presses, two ripples | as `move` | | `hover(sel)` | moves and rests (`.is-hover` on the target) | `dur` .9, `hold` .6 | | `type(sel, text)` | characters appear in `sel` at a human, uneven pace; `.is-caret` while typing, then blinking | `cps` 13, `rhythm` (below), `lead` (s of steady caret before the first key), `caret` (s it blinks after the last key, 1.6), `blink` (absolute time it goes) | | `stream(sel)` | each match appears in turn, like output arriving: gets `.is-in`, and `--in` 0→1 over `dur`. A match's `data-tour-wait="1.2"` adds that pause before it (a slow step) | `every` .06 s, `jitter` .5 (±50 % of `every`; 0 for an exact beat), `dur` .08 | | `drag(handle, o)` | moves to the handle, presses, then drives a value while the cursor stays on the handle | `approach` .8, `dur` 1.2, `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el` to put the property on another element), `text: [sel, v => label]`, or `onto: sel` to carry the handle itself there | | `scroll(sel, to)` | scrolls an element; `to` is px, `'50%'`, `'end'` or a selector inside it | `dur` 1.4, `offset` 16 | | `key(keys)` | key caps on screen, e.g. `key(['⌘', 'K'])` | `dur` .9, `hold` 1.4 | | `pause(s)` | a beat | | | `tap(sel)` | the same step as `click`; reads better in a touch film | as `click` | | `longpress(sel)` | moves, presses and holds; it fires (`.is-press` stays on, a ripple) after `hold`, and the finger stays down `lift` longer while the next steps start (open a context menu there) | `dur` .9, `hold` .7, `lift` .35 | | `swipe(sel, o)` | a finger flick that starts on `sel`: lands, travels `by` [dx, dy] window px speeding up, lifts while still moving. What it moves follows it 1:1, then coasts to rest over `coast` s with the speed it was let go at. `scroll: to` scrolls `sel` (or `in: sel`) to `to` (px, `'50%'`, `'end'`, a selector; `offset`); `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el`) drives a CSS variable instead (a carousel, a sheet dragged down), `follow` (.45) of it under the finger | `approach` .7, `by` [0, -220], `dur` .36, `coast` .8 (0: a slow drag that ends at rest), `settle` (when the next step starts, `coast` × .5) | `type`'s `rhythm`: unset is the even, slightly uneven pace it always had. `'human'` types like a person at a keyboard: a beat between words, a reach for symbols (`- / . : =`), a pause after punctuation, doubled letters run together, the odd hesitation. `'stream'` lands the text in chunks of 1–5 characters, the way a model's reply arrives. `stream()` is for whole lines or blocks; hide them in CSS until `.is-in` (`.line{display:none}.line.is-in{display:block}`) so they take space only once they've arrived. The cursor's path between targets is a smootherstep glide with a slight bow (direction-dependent, never a straight line) and a slightly early peak speed, like a hand. It never teleports: each move starts where the last one ended. **A finger instead of a cursor.** `pointer: 'touch'` in the script (or `data-pointer="touch"` on the root, `?pointer=touch`) swaps the arrow for a fingertip: a soft translucent dot, 44 window px, that is part of the screen, so it zooms with it. Give each touch a beat: the `dur` before it is the hand travelling. Restyle the dot with `--tour-touch` / `--tour-touch-down`. `demo/phone` is the worked example. **More than one pointer.** Any pointer step with `by: 'agent'` moves a second cursor on its own track (any name works; steps without `by` move the usual one, `'main'`). Its markup is yours to edit: the film (the diary inside the frame, the rail under it), then the offers, how it goes, proof, questions, the booking, the footer kit/ placeholder kit: tokens, .ph frames, buttons, notes (press N to hide notes) office-hours/section.css the stage, the rail, the diary in its three layouts, and the page (.oh-…) office-hours/script.js the film: three chapters, the offer it picks, what the visitor writes office-hours/section.js fills the coming week's dates, plays the film once it's on screen, the booking's logic office-hours/section.html the markup as it came (index.html has a filled-in copy; edit index.html) tour/ the engine (tour.js, tour.css), snapshot.py, README.md; don't edit ``` (In the StyleFeatures repo, `python3 templates/scaffolds/sections/demo/tour/export.py --format office-hours` makes this layout.) Serve the folder with any static server, e.g. `python3 -m http.server 8000`. ## 1. Gather their things (before writing anything) Ask the person for what you can't find, and confirm anything you found before it goes public. Look in this order: - **Their booking link.** Cal.com, SavvyCal, TidyCal, Calendly, Acuity, Google Calendar appointment pages, Zcal, a `book`/`call` page on their site, the link in their email signature. Note **one URL per offer** if their tool has separate event types (`cal.com/name/intro`, `cal.com/name/session`), and whether it can be embedded (most give an inline-embed URL or snippet). That link is the ending of the page; the diary on top is a picture of it. - **Their offers.** The event types in that tool are the honest list: name, length, the description they wrote. Also their site's Services / Work with me / Coaching page, a rate card PDF, a proposal template. Take **two or three**, with the **lengths they really sell** ("20 min", "45 min", "3 h", "a day"). Rates **only if they already publish them**; otherwise the rate line is deleted, never estimated. - **Their hours.** When they actually take calls: which days, which hours, which time zone (an IANA name such as `Europe/Lisbon`, `America/New_York`). Their scheduler's availability settings say this exactly. Ask what they never do ("no calls on Friday afternoons", "mornings are for writing"): that becomes the handwritten note in the diary. - **Who they help, with what.** Their bio on LinkedIn, X, their site's About, their newsletter. You need one sentence in the shape "I help *who* with *what*", in their words, shortened if it must be, never rewritten into marketing. - **How working together goes.** What happens before a call (a questionnaire? nothing?), on it, after it (notes, a plan, a recording, an invoice) and when. Their onboarding email or welcome doc usually has it. - **Proof.** Testimonials they already publish (their site, LinkedIn recommendations, Google reviews, a Senja/Testimonial wall), with the person's name and role. **Only real ones, and only with permission.** Client logos only where the client agreed to be named. If there are none, delete the proof section; don't leave fakes. - **Questions people really ask.** Their FAQ page, or ask them for the three questions they answer most in email. - **Their look.** If they have a site, take its fonts and its one accent colour (CSS variables, a theme file) and set `--oh-ink` (the fountain-pen blue) to it. Otherwise keep the kit's warm paper and the ink. Therapists, coaches and anyone working with private clients: the diary shows **patterns, not people**. Busy time is hatched and never labelled, and nothing on the page hints at who else is in the week. ## 2. Fill the diary (inside the frame) The diary is `.oh-diary` inside `[data-tour-window]` in `index.html`, built in design pixels with three layouts from one set of markup (`office-hours/section.css`): **wide** 1200 × 740 (margin on the left, Monday–Friday), **square** 800 × 700 (`.is-square`: the margin becomes a band over the week; 1:1 recordings) and **tall** 480 × 800 (`.is-tall`: the margin on top, Wednesday–Friday only; phones and 9:16). Check all three after every change. - **The margin** `.oh-margin`: `.oh-name` (their name exactly as they write it), `.oh-help` ("I help … with …"), and the offers `.oh-offer` ×2–3: `data-len` is the length in minutes (it decides which times fade in the film), `data-name` the name, then the name, the length as they say it, and one short line. Keep the `data-tour="offer-…"` hooks. The little month and "Times in …" are filled by `section.js`. - **Time zone.** Put their IANA zone on the root: `
`, and replace every "your city's time" with how they'd say it ("Lisbon time"). With `data-tz` empty the page uses the visitor's own zone. - **The week** `.oh-cols`: one `.oh-col` per day. Each time is a box with `style="--s:10;--m:60"` (start in hours, 13.5 = 13:30; length in minutes) and its label. Open times: `10:001 h`. Busy: ``, no text. Draw **their real pattern** for a typical week, not their actual appointments. The grid runs 9:00–17:00 (`--h0:9;--hours:8` on `.oh-diary`, and the hour labels in `.oh-hours`); change all three together for other hours. - **The booked time** `[data-tour="slot-thu"]` is the one the film books. It holds the lit band, the entry it becomes, the slip, the invite card and the camera's zone. Move the whole element to another day or hour if Thursday at ten isn't a time they'd offer; `section.js` reads its column and label for every date on the slip and the card. - **The handwritten note** `.oh-hand`: one thing they never do, in their words, or delete it. - **The invite card** `.oh-invite`: the offer's name, `{{call_how}}` (how calls happen: "Video call · the link is in the invite", "Phone call · I'll ring you", "At the studio, 12 Example Street" only if they meet in person and say so). - Dates fill in from the coming week. To pin a week (for a recording you'll redo later), set `data-week="2026-11-09"` on the root. **Static HTML/CSS only** inside the frame. The diary is a picture the film moves; the real booking is at the end. ## 3. The script (`office-hours/script.js`) It tells the booking in three chapters (*what you need*, *a time that suits*, *in the diary*), about 33 s. Adjust it to them rather than rewriting it: - `FILM_OFFER` is the offer the visitor picks: their most common one, usually the middle one. - `WHO` and `ABOUT` are what the visitor writes on the slip. Keep `WHO` a plain first name and make `ABOUT` the kind of thing their clients really bring them, in a client's words ("Our launch plan needs a second pair of eyes", "My daughter's maths exam is in May", "We need a pricing model before the board meeting"). Never a real client's name or problem. - Chapter titles (a few words, one ``) and captions (one short sentence per action) in their voice. - Every action visibly changes something; one push-in per chapter, then `unzoom()`. `mark('still')` is the frame reduced motion shows: the week with the entry written in. ## 4. Fill the page under the film - **The rail** under the frame: `.oh-band` (`{{band_title}}`, `{{band_line}}`) and the closing frame `.oh-end` (name, their booking address and email, shown at the end of the recording). - **Offers** `#offers`: each `.oh-off` with `style="--m:45"` (minutes, drawn on a three-hour rule), the length set large, the name, two plain sentences on what happens and what they leave with, who it's for, the rate **only if published**, and "Book this" (`data-offer` = its index, which picks it in the booking). - **How it goes** `#how`: three steps, dated the way they'd say it ("Before", "On the call", "Within two days"). - **Proof** `#proof`: real logos (SVG or a clean PNG on transparent, grey them with `filter: grayscale(1)` if they're loud) and one real quote with name and role, or delete the section. - **Questions** `#faq`: three to five, answered in two sentences each. - **The booking** `#book`: put their scheduler's embed URL on `.oh-embed`: `data-embed="https://cal.com/name"` for one link, or `data-embed-0`, `-1`, `-2` for one per offer (the picker switches between them). `section.js` puts it in an iframe; use the tool's **inline embed** URL (Cal.com: the event URL with `?embed=true` or their embed snippet's link; SavvyCal and TidyCal: the inline embed link). If their tool only offers a script snippet, paste it inside `.oh-embed` in place of the `.ph` and leave `data-embed` empty. If they have no scheduler, delete `.oh-embed`: the email fallback (with the offer and any time picked in the diary) becomes the booking. - Clicking an open time or an offer in the diary (after or during the film) brings the visitor here with it chosen, and the email fallback carries it. Keep the open times honest for that reason. - Delete every ``, set the page `` ("Name: book a call") and the meta description (their "I help … with …" line). ## 5. Check it - `index.html?t=14` freezes any moment. Check the middle of each chapter and just after each action: the cursor sits on what it clicked, the times that fade are the ones too short, the slip is whole inside the frame, the card lands squarely on the time and becomes the entry. - `?record&ratio=16:9&t=…`, `?record&ratio=1:1&t=…`, `?record&ratio=9:16&t=…`, and the page at 1440 × 900 and on a 390-wide phone: no sideways scroll, nothing important cut, the diary legible. - With reduced motion: one calm frame, the week with the entry written in. - Nothing left that is lorem, a placeholder you meant to replace, a rate they don't publish, a testimonial without permission, or a hint of who their other clients are. ## 6. Hand it over: record and post End by giving the person this, with the link filled in: 1. Open **`index.html?record&ratio=16:9`** (served, e.g. `http://localhost:8000/?record&ratio=16:9`) in a browser window large enough for a crisp stage: 1920 × 1080 or larger on a Retina display. 2. Record it with **Monet Shot**: choose the browser window, crop to the stage, park the real pointer off the window (the film draws its own cursor). It holds on the first frame for 1.2 s, plays once and stops on the closing frame. Monet Shot adds no zooms of its own, because the clicks aren't real; if you'd rather place zooms on its timeline, open `?record&ratio=16:9&camera=off` so you don't get both. 3. Export H.264 MP4 and post it to X with one line and the link to the booking. **16:9** reads best on desktop and in quote posts; `ratio=1:1` takes more of the phone feed; `ratio=9:16` is for stories. Record each ratio separately; the diary lays itself out again for each, so never crop one into another. 4. X takes MP4 (H.264, AAC) up to 2 min 20 s and 512 MB. The captions are burned in, because X autoplays muted.

# tour.js: the demo-film engine One engine for every StyleFeatures demo film. A template supplies a window with a product inside it and a script; the engine plays it with a fake cursor, a camera, chapter cards and captions, and drives it from a scroll, a clock, a screen recorder or a frozen `?t=`. Files: | file | what it is | edit it? | |---|---|---| | `tour.js` | the engine: step builders, `Tour`, `include()` | no, it's shared by every format | | `tour.css` | the engine's look: chromes, cursor, card, caption, keys, controls, record stage | no; restyle through its tokens | | `script.js` | this film's script | yes | | `section.html` / `section.css` | this film's band, closing frame and product | yes | | `snapshot.py` | harvests a live screen into a static fragment | no | | `export.py` | copies the whole format out as a standalone folder | no | | `AGENT.md` | the brief for the coding agent that fills it in | read it | Everything on screen is a pure function of one number, `t`, in seconds. Each frame the engine works out the product's state at `t` (classes, attributes, text, CSS variables, scroll positions), the camera, the cursor and the overlays, then writes only what changed. Nothing depends on what happened in earlier frames, so any moment renders on its own, the same way every time. ## Markup ```html
… your product, built at 1200 × 750 design pixels …
…
…
``` The engine adds the chrome, the cursor, ripples, the chapter card, the caption line, key caps, and the driver's controls. The opening band (`data-tour-band`) slides away in the first `intro` seconds; the closing frame (`data-tour-end`) gets `--in` 0→1 at the end and its own CSS decides what that looks like. The root also carries `--tour-band` (1 → 0 over the intro), `--tour-out` (0 → 1 over the outro) and `--tour-p` (0 → 1 over the whole film) for a format's own CSS. `data-tour-band="css"` stops the engine sliding the band away; the format fades or moves it from `--tour-band` instead. **A frame the format draws: `data-tour-frame`.** Put an element with `data-tour-frame` in the stage and lay it out in CSS (a phone's glass, a mat around a screenshot, a different box per ratio). The engine fits the window to it exactly, clips the camera to it (with its `border-radius`), and every zoom stays inside it: the window always covers the frame, so a push-in never shows what's around it. The outro then leaves the window where it is (use `--tour-out` to do something else). Give the frame the window's aspect ratio. `demo/phone` (the glass, beside the text or under it) and `demo/launch-note` (a mat on the page, a different box per recording ratio) use it. ### Window chromes: `data-chrome` | value | looks like | typical `data-size` | |---|---|---| | `browser` | traffic lights, back/forward, an address pill (`data-url`), share/new icons | `1200x750` | | `app` | a macOS title bar with traffic lights and a centred `data-title` | `1200x760` | | `phone` | a dark bezel, a status bar with the time and a notch | `390x844` | | `none` | just rounded corners | anything | | `terminal` | a warm charcoal window, traffic lights, a centred `data-title`; tokens `--tour-term-bg/-bar/-ink/-dim` | `780x548` | **Windows inside the window.** Any element inside the window with a `data-chrome` gets that chrome too, and a frame (`display:flex`, rounded, clipped). With `data-chrome="none"` on the outer window (made transparent in your CSS) it becomes a desk holding, say, a terminal and a browser; the camera pans between them with `zoom()` (`demo/terminal` does this). **A second design size for tall stages.** `data-size-tall="440x820"` on the window (or `sizeTall: [440, 820]` in the script) is used whenever the stage is taller than wide (W/H < .8: phones, 9:16 recordings). The root gets `.is-tall` before anything is measured, so your CSS can re-lay the product for it (stack two panes, say) and the script's targets follow. `demo/split` stacks its panes this way. **A third for squarish stages.** `data-size-square="760x760"` (or `sizeSquare: [760, 760]`) is used when .8 ≤ W/H < 1.15 (1:1 recordings, square-ish windows), and the root gets `.is-square` the same way. Without it those stages use the wide size, as before. `demo/agentic` has all three: a tiled desk (wide), and one live window beside (square) or above (tall) its run sheet. **A height that follows the frame: `auto`.** `data-size="580xauto"` (or `size: [580, 'auto']`, and the same for `sizeTall`) fixes the window's width and takes its height from the `data-tour-frame` at every layout, so the window always has the frame's shape: a full-height column on a wide page, the whole screen on a phone, any recording ratio. For products that read top to bottom (a chat, a feed, a transcript). `demo/chat` and `demo/mcp` use it. Build the product at the design size in plain CSS pixels. The engine scales the whole window, so text stays real text and stays sharp at any zoom. ### Hooks `'@name'` anywhere in a selector means `[data-tour="name"]`. Put `data-tour="…"` on the things the script points at. Pointer targets also choose the cursor: links, buttons, `role=button|tab|switch` get the hand, inputs and `data-tour-cursor="text"` get the I-beam, the rest the arrow (`data-tour-cursor="arrow|pointer|text"` overrides it). While the cursor rests on a target, that target has `.is-hover`; while it's pressed, `.is-press`. Style both so clicks read. ## The script ```js import { click, type, show, hide, set, tween, zoom, unzoom, chapter, caption, pause } from './tour.js'; export default { size: [1200, 750], // window design size (or data-size on the window) enter: [.84, .97], // where the cursor comes in from, as fractions of the window intro: 1.3, // seconds for the opening band to clear (0: no band) outro: 4.5, // seconds held on the closing frame settle: .6, // pause between the last step and the outro still: 17.4, // the moment reduced motion shows fit: [.92, .88, .5], // optional: see below steps: [ … ], }; ``` `fit: [w, h, y]` is for a stage that holds nothing but the window (a panel beside text, with no card or band over it): the window may take `w` of the stage's width and `h` of its height, centred at `y` (default .5), and push-ins aim at the middle of the frame. Without it the page layout leaves room for the card and band (`[.74, .7, .47]`). It never changes `?record`. `demo/chapters` uses it. Steps run in order on one clock. **Pointer steps** take time and the next step waits for them. **Side steps** start at the current moment and the next step starts with them, so `click('@create'), hide('@modal'), show('@toast')` hides the modal and shows the toast as the click lands. Every step takes: `at: 12.5` pin it to an absolute time · `wait: .4` start this much later · `parallel: true` (pointer steps) don't hold up the next step · `block: true` (side steps) do hold it up. ### Pointer steps | step | what happens | options (defaults) | |---|---|---| | `move(sel)` | glides there on a gentle arc, smootherstep | `dur` .9, `aim` [x, y] fractions of the target, `cursor` | | `click(sel)` | moves, presses (cursor shrinks, target gets `.is-press`), ripple | as `move` | | `dblclick(sel)` | moves, two presses, two ripples | as `move` | | `hover(sel)` | moves and rests (`.is-hover` on the target) | `dur` .9, `hold` .6 | | `type(sel, text)` | characters appear in `sel` at a human, uneven pace; `.is-caret` while typing, then blinking | `cps` 13, `rhythm` (below), `lead` (s of steady caret before the first key), `caret` (s it blinks after the last key, 1.6), `blink` (absolute time it goes) | | `stream(sel)` | each match appears in turn, like output arriving: gets `.is-in`, and `--in` 0→1 over `dur`. A match's `data-tour-wait="1.2"` adds that pause before it (a slow step) | `every` .06 s, `jitter` .5 (±50 % of `every`; 0 for an exact beat), `dur` .08 | | `drag(handle, o)` | moves to the handle, presses, then drives a value while the cursor stays on the handle | `approach` .8, `dur` 1.2, `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el` to put the property on another element), `text: [sel, v => label]`, or `onto: sel` to carry the handle itself there | | `scroll(sel, to)` | scrolls an element; `to` is px, `'50%'`, `'end'` or a selector inside it | `dur` 1.4, `offset` 16 | | `key(keys)` | key caps on screen, e.g. `key(['⌘', 'K'])` | `dur` .9, `hold` 1.4 | | `pause(s)` | a beat | | | `tap(sel)` | the same step as `click`; reads better in a touch film | as `click` | | `longpress(sel)` | moves, presses and holds; it fires (`.is-press` stays on, a ripple) after `hold`, and the finger stays down `lift` longer while the next steps start (open a context menu there) | `dur` .9, `hold` .7, `lift` .35 | | `swipe(sel, o)` | a finger flick that starts on `sel`: lands, travels `by` [dx, dy] window px speeding up, lifts while still moving. What it moves follows it 1:1, then coasts to rest over `coast` s with the speed it was let go at. `scroll: to` scrolls `sel` (or `in: sel`) to `to` (px, `'50%'`, `'end'`, a selector; `offset`); `prop` + `from` + `to` (+ `el`) drives a CSS variable instead (a carousel, a sheet dragged down), `follow` (.45) of it under the finger | `approach` .7, `by` [0, -220], `dur` .36, `coast` .8 (0: a slow drag that ends at rest), `settle` (when the next step starts, `coast` × .5) | `type`'s `rhythm`: unset is the even, slightly uneven pace it always had. `'human'` types like a person at a keyboard: a beat between words, a reach for symbols (`- / . : =`), a pause after punctuation, doubled letters run together, the odd hesitation. `'stream'` lands the text in chunks of 1–5 characters, the way a model's reply arrives. `stream()` is for whole lines or blocks; hide them in CSS until `.is-in` (`.line{display:none}.line.is-in{display:block}`) so they take space only once they've arrived. The cursor's path between targets is a smootherstep glide with a slight bow (direction-dependent, never a straight line) and a slightly early peak speed, like a hand. It never teleports: each move starts where the last one ended. **A finger instead of a cursor.** `pointer: 'touch'` in the script (or `data-pointer="touch"` on the root, `?pointer=touch`) swaps the arrow for a fingertip: a soft translucent dot, 44 window px, that is part of the screen, so it zooms with it. It is unseen between touches (a hand travelling isn't on the glass); a shadow gathers for a fifth of a second before contact, the dot flattens and darkens while pressed (`.is-down` on `.tour-cur`), and lifts away. `drag` and `swipe` carry it across the glass. Give each touch a beat: the `dur` before it is the hand travelling. Restyle the dot with `--tour-touch` / `--tour-touch-down`. `demo/phone` is the worked example. **More than one pointer.** Any pointer step with `by: 'agent'` moves a second cursor on its own track (any name works; steps without `by` move the usual one, `'main'`). Describe each in the script: ```js pointers: { main: { label: 'You', idle: 1.4 }, // a tag on the person's cursor; it fades after 1.4 s still agent: { label: 'Agent', look: 'agent', bow: .2, enter: [.33, .2] }, }, steps: [ click('@search', { by: 'agent', tag: 'search_code' }), …, click('@approve', { from: [.99, 1.03] }) ] ``` A second pointer is an arrow in `--tour-agent` (look `'agent'`) with a label tag beside it; `tag` on a step adds a word to that label from then on (the tool it's using, "waiting for you"). `bow` scales the curve of its path (0 is a straight, machine-like line), `enter` is where it first appears, `shapes: true` lets it take the hand and I-beam too. `idle: s` fades a pointer out once it has been still that long and back in when it next moves; `from: [x, y]` (fractions of the window) on a step starts that move there instead, so a hand can come back in from off the edge. Each pointer's clicks ripple in its own colour (`.tour-ring[data-who]`), and `.tour-cur[data-who="…"]` lets a page hide one (`demo/agentic` hides the person's cursor on the live page, where the visitor is the person). Touch mode (`pointer: 'touch'`) applies to the main pointer only. ### Side steps | step | what happens | options | |---|---|---| | `show(sel)` / `hide(sel)` | tweens `--in` to 1 / 0 on every match; your CSS uses `opacity: var(--in)` etc. | `dur` .35 / .28, `stagger` | | `set(sel, changes)` | instant: `{class: '+on -off'}`, `{text: 'Copied'}`, `{'--x': 2}`, `{'data-view': 'room'}`, `{attr: null}` removes | | | `tween(sel, prop, from, to)` | animates a CSS variable, `'text'` (with `fmt`) or `'scrollTop'` | `dur` .45, `fmt`, `stagger` | | `zoom(sel, z)` | camera pushes in on the target. `z` a number, or `'fit'` to frame the element at `fill` of the frame | `dur` 1.3, `fill` .66 (or `[wide, stacked]`, e.g. `[.76, .96]`: tighter on 1:1 and phones, where the window is small), `aim`, `max` 2.6 (the most a `'fit'` may push in: raise it for a big window such as a whole board), `arc` 0 (0–1: pull back by that share mid-flight and push in again, so a long pan reads as a camera crossing; `demo/canvas`) | | `unzoom()` | camera back to the whole window | `dur` 1.3 | | `chapter(n, title, line)` | the card: `'02 / 05'`, a title with one `` word, one line; until the next chapter | `until` | | `caption(text)` | the caption line, until the next caption | `dur` 4 | | `mark(name)` | nothing on screen: a named moment. `tour.api.marks` lists them in order (`{ t, name }`) and `marks[name]` is that moment's time, so a page can seek to one or stop at the next (`demo/chat`'s beats, `demo/mcp`'s tabs) | | `show`, `hide` and `tween` take `ease`: `'out'` (decelerate), `'ios'` (a critically damped spring, UIKit's pushes and sheets), `'spring'` (overshoots by about 3 %), `'linear'`, or any `(t) => t` function. The default is smootherstep. The curves are exported as `eases`. `data-tour-follow` on a scrolling element (a terminal, a chat thread, a log) keeps its newest content in view every frame, so lines that `stream()` in push the old ones up. `data-tour-grow` on an element that should take height as it arrives (a message in a thread, a folded panel): the engine measures its natural height into `--h` (design px, innermost first, before targets are measured, and again on every relayout), so your CSS can open it with `--in` and let go once it's in: `max-height: max(calc(var(--in) * var(--h)), calc((var(--in) - .999) * 1e7px))`. Rows arrive smoothly and may change size afterwards. `../_chat/chat.css` is the worked example. Elements that `show()` controls should start hidden in CSS (`--in: 0`). Anything the script changes is reset when you seek backwards, because every value is recomputed from `t`. ### The camera `zoom` pushes in on a point and keeps the window filling the frame: it borrows Monet Shot's fit clamp, so a push-in never pans past the window's edge (the window is either wholly inside the frame or covers it). Zoom levels move on a log scale, so in and out feel even. Numbers are multiplied by 1.15 on portrait stages, where the window is small (not inside a `data-tour-frame`, which the window always fills). `?camera=off` turns all push-ins off. On stacked stages (1:1, 9:16, phones) the cursor fades out rather than being drawn outside the window's frame. ### Measuring Targets are measured in the window's own pixels, against the product as it is at the moment each step happens (so a button inside a modal that opens two steps earlier is measured with the modal open), and measured again whenever the layout can change: fonts loading, the stage resizing, your CSS. Edit the product freely; the script follows. ## The card and caption keep out of the way The chapter card and the caption never sit on what the tour is doing. Each frame the engine checks the cursor (or fingertip) and any text being typed (`type`) or streamed in (`stream`), with its last second after. If the card would cover it, the card slides to the other side of the stage; if both sides are busy it steps out, and it comes home once the spot has been clear for .8 s. The caption lifts to the top. Outside `?record` the card carries a × that hides the cards for the rest of the visit; recordings have none. Nothing to configure. In stacked layouts (phones, 9:16) the card already sits under the window, so nothing moves. ## Drivers | driver | how | when | |---|---|---| | `scroll` (default) | `data-driver="scroll"`. The section gets tall, the stage pins, scroll maps to `t`. The gate starts an auto-play drift at real speed. With `data-lock` (default on) wheel, touch and keys can't skip the film while it drifts; the Auto-play switch is the way out. A film at the very top of the page holds the page still until the first click, tap or key. | the opening of a launch page, Monet Shot style | | `play` | `data-driver="play"`. A 100svh stage with a play button, a scrubber with chapter ticks and a timecode. No gate, controls or scroll handling: it draws `t = 0` and waits. The tour's clicks are drawn, not real, so Monet Shot sees none and adds no zooms of its own. The tour's camera therefore stays **on** by default. If you would rather place zooms yourself on Monet Shot's timeline, use `&camera=off` and you won't get double zooms. - Monet Shot draws its own cursor from the real pointer. Park the real pointer off the recorded window (or set Monet Shot's cursor to hidden) so only the tour's cursor shows. From script: `window.tour` has `seek(t)`, `play()`, `pause()`, `load(script)`, `t`, `duration`, `chapters` and `ready` (a promise that resolves once fonts are in and everything is measured). The root gets a `tour:end` event whenever `play()` reaches the end (any driver). **Several tours in one recorded frame.** A format whose recording is more than one film (two windows racing in `demo/versus`, a whole slide deck in `demo/deck`) makes its own element the record stage and drives the tours itself: ```js import { Tour, recordStage } from './tour.js'; const box = q.has('record') ? recordStage(root) : null; // root becomes the ratio's box, centred on near-black, the rest hidden const a = new Tour(filmA, scriptA, { driver: 'manual', record: 'page' }); // no record stage or auto-play of its own a.render(t); // the page decides t, every frame ``` `recordStage(el)` does for `el` what `?record` does for a single film (the `tour-record` and `sf-clean` classes, `--rw`/`--rh` from `&ratio=`, kept current on resize) and returns `{ w, h, ratio }`. `{ record: 'page' }` on a Tour means: in `?record` stay on the manual driver and let the page play it (captions follow `captions` as usual). Without `?record` it changes nothing.
